questions.stem: Under which Article of the Constitution is the office of the President of India established?
questions.explanation: Article 52: 'There shall be a President of India.' Article 54 deals with election; Article 61 deals with impeachment. The President is the ceremonial Head of State and supreme commander of the defence forces (Article 53).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The minimum age required for a person to be eligible for election as President of India is:
questions.explanation: Article 58: candidate must be (a) citizen of India; (b) ≥ 35 years old; (c) qualified for election as Lok Sabha member; (d) not holding office of profit under Union/State/local authority. Compare: Vice-President also 35, RS member 30, LS member 25, MLA 25, MLC 30. Governor also 35.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of:

options.option_text: Only elected MPs of both Houses
Elected MPs of both Houses + elected MLAs of State Legislative Assemblies
All MPs (elected + nominated) + all MLAs (elected + nominated)
Direct election by universal adult franchise

questions.explanation: Article 54: electoral college = elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (post-70th Amendment 1992, also includes Delhi and Puducherry). NOMINATED members (both RS/LS and Council) DO NOT vote. Method: proportional representation by single transferable vote, secret ballot. Vote value of each MP/MLA is calculated to maintain parity between Union and States.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Who administers the oath of office to the President of India?

options.option_text: The Chief Justice of India (or in his absence, the senior-most SC judge)
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.explanation: Article 60: the CJI administers the oath to the President. If the CJI is unavailable, the senior-most SC judge available does so. VP's oath, in contrast, is administered by the President (Article 69). Governor's oath by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court (Article 159).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Who was the first President of India, and for how many terms did he hold office?
questions.explanation: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (26 Jan 1950 – 13 May 1962) was India's FIRST President and the ONLY one to serve TWO FULL TERMS (1950-57 and 1957-62). He was also the President of the Constituent Assembly (1946-50). Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (2nd, 1962-67). Dr. Zakir Hussain (3rd, 1967-69, died in office). V.V. Giri (4th, acting then elected, 1969-74). As of 2026 there have been 15 Presidents; Droupadi Murmu (15th, since 2022) is the first tribal & 2nd woman President.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The term of office of the President of India is:

options.option_text: 5 years from the date he enters upon his office

questions.explanation: Article 56: President holds office for 5 years from the date of entering office. Eligible for re-election any number of times (unlike the US 22nd Amendment limit). Tenure NOT tied to Lok Sabha. 6-year tenure is for the CAG, not the President (common trap).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The procedure for impeachment of the President of India is laid down in which Article?
questions.explanation: Article 61: President can be impeached for 'violation of the Constitution'. Procedure: (1) charge must be signed by ≥ 1/4 of total members of either House + 14-day prior notice; (2) passed by ≥ 2/3 of total membership of the moving House; (3) other House investigates (President can appear personally); (4) the 2nd House must also pass by ≥ 2/3 of total membership → removal. No Indian President has ever been impeached. Nominated members of RS/LS CAN participate in impeachment (they're part of Parliament), unlike in election.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a DISCRETIONARY power of the President of India (where he can act without cabinet advice)?

options.option_text: Appointing a PM when no party has clear majority
Dissolving Lok Sabha when CoM has lost majority
Pocket veto (indefinitely withholding assent to a non-Money Bill)

questions.explanation: National Emergency under Article 352 requires WRITTEN recommendation from the Cabinet (not just PM) per the 44th Amendment, 1978 — NOT discretionary. Discretionary powers include: (a) appointing PM when no clear majority; (b) dismissal of CoM that loses confidence but doesn't resign; (c) dissolving LS when CoM has lost majority; (d) POCKET VETO — sitting on a non-Money bill indefinitely without signing or returning; (e) advice to CoM to reconsider a bill (suspensive veto) once. Essentially 'nominal' in most matters, discretionary in a few.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The pardoning power of the President of India is granted under which Article?
questions.explanation: Article 72: President's pardoning power includes PARDON (full forgiveness — removes conviction), COMMUTATION (substitution with a lighter form — e.g., death to life imprisonment), REMISSION (reduces period without changing character), RESPITE (lighter punishment due to special circumstances — e.g., pregnancy), REPRIEVE (temporary stay of execution). President's jurisdiction: death sentences (EXCLUSIVE), court-martial sentences (EXCLUSIVE), Union List offences. Governor's pardoning (Article 161) excludes death sentences. Difference: only President can pardon DEATH sentences.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The ORDINANCE-making power of the President is granted under which Article, and the ordinance ceases to operate within how many weeks of Parliament's reassembly?
questions.explanation: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is NOT in session. Maximum duration: must be laid before Parliament when it reassembles; ceases to operate 6 weeks after reassembly (unless approved by Parliament, it disappears). Equivalent for Governor: Article 213. Ordinances have the same force as an Act of Parliament during their life. Famous case: D.C. Wadhwa v State of Bihar (1987) — SC struck down re-promulgation of ordinances without parliamentary approval as a 'fraud on the Constitution'. Krishna Kumar Singh case (2017) reaffirmed this.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following was NOT a previous profession of an Indian President?
questions.explanation: No Indian President has been a military general (by profession). Professions of notable Indian Presidents: lawyers/barristers (Rajendra Prasad, V.V. Giri, Zakir Hussain), academics/philosophers (Radhakrishnan, Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed), scientist (Kalam, 11th — DRDO missile programme, 'People's President'), politicians/FM (Pranab Mukherjee, 13th — Congress stalwart), farmers/Dalit leader (K.R. Narayanan, first Dalit President), Telugu leader (Neelam Sanjiva Reddy), tribal activist (Droupadi Murmu, 15th, Santhal from Odisha). India's only woman Presidents: Pratibha Patil (12th, 2007-12) + Droupadi Murmu (15th, 2022-).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The President's VETO powers in India include all EXCEPT:

options.option_text: Qualified veto (vetoed bill needs 2/3 to override)

questions.explanation: Indian President has THREE veto powers: (1) ABSOLUTE — used for private member bills, bills passed by CoM that subsequently resigns; (2) SUSPENSIVE — return bill (except Money Bill) to Parliament for reconsideration; if Parliament repasses with or without amendments, President must assent (Article 111); (3) POCKET — sit on the bill indefinitely (no constitutional time limit). The USA Constitution has QUALIFIED veto (2/3 supermajority override needed); India does NOT. Famous pocket veto: PRESIDENT ZAIL SINGH on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill 1986.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Who among the following was the ONLY President to be UNANIMOUSLY elected (unopposed)?
questions.explanation: Neelam SANJIVA REDDY (6th President, 1977-82) is the ONLY Indian President elected UNOPPOSED — no one filed opposing nominations. He was also the ONLY President from Andhra Pradesh (Telugu). Interestingly, he had LOST the 1969 presidential election (to V.V. Giri, who ran as independent against the official Congress candidate Reddy — a pivotal moment in Indira Gandhi's rise and the Congress split). Eight years later, Reddy won unopposed as the Janata Party's nominee.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The President of India is part of Parliament (Article 79). What are the two Houses?
questions.explanation: Article 79: 'There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States [RAJYA SABHA] and the House of the People [LOK SABHA].' So Parliament includes the President as a constituent part. Important implication: a bill becomes law only after President's assent (Article 111). In the UK, similarly, the Monarch is part of Parliament ('King/Queen in Parliament'). In contrast, the US Constitution makes Congress and the President separate bodies.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: If the office of both the President AND Vice-President is vacant, who performs the duties of the President?

options.option_text: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chief Justice of India (or in his absence, senior-most SC judge)

questions.explanation: Per the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969: if both President and VP offices are vacant simultaneously, the CHIEF JUSTICE OF INDIA discharges the functions of the President. If the CJI is unable to act, the senior-most SC judge available does so. This happened ONCE — in 1969, when President Dr. Zakir Hussain died in office (May 3, 1969) and then acting President V.V. Giri resigned (July 20, 1969) to contest; Justice M. HIDAYATULLAH (CJI) served as Acting President from 20 July to 24 August 1969.
